artboards.title: Alternative · sections read their credit count

annotations.text:
What is there today.

One panel with everything on it. The hull is walked on the top row, five flight bars read under it, the credit tray sits under those, and then every slot the hull can spend on runs down the rest of the glass under three band labels: gun, bomb, rack.

On an Apex that is 762 points of panel against the 782 an 810-point window has to give it: it fits by twenty and scrolls on anything shorter, a phone included. What goes off the top first is the tray, so a pilot stepping a slot near the foot is spending a purse they cannot see.

Five rows and a reset fit any window without scrolling, and the tray stops being the third strip of the content and becomes part of the panel.

The rules these boards follow.

The tray is chrome. It is drawn by the panel, under the back bar, above everything the page is about, and it is the same seven diamonds on the menu and on all five sections. There is no scroll position left that could take it away.

It does not hold still. A panel is as tall as what it holds and stands on the bottom margin it slid out of, so a section of four rows sits lower than a menu of six and its tray rides down with its own head. What is fixed is the tray's place in a panel, not its place on the screen.

A section reads what it holds, in the games list's voice: menu_row draws a detail at TYPE.BODY in pal.MUTE, hard against the right of the type column, in the face the numbers in flight are set in. That is what "4v4 3:00" wears on the zone stop, and it is what "2 rounds, bouncing" wears here.

Body carries the stats twice: the hull's five bars stand under the row that names it on the menu, and the section itself turns one ship at a time with its five rows read out one to a line underneath. The bars take a floor, so the hull at the bottom of a row draws a stub rather than nothing.

Nothing new in the language. A section row opens, which is the caret every stop already wears, and the rows inside are decision 104's six ends unchanged, minus the walker the roster no longer needs.

Where the five came from.

Four are the sections menu.tune_rows already builds, under Chris's words: flight becomes body, gun becomes guns, bomb becomes bombs, rack becomes specials. Which rows appear inside each is still the core's answer, not a list written in the client, so a zone that gives a hull no bomb rack opens a bombs section with nothing in it rather than one nobody remembered to hide.

Body is the one section that is a choice rather than a set of slots, and it took three shapes: a walker with no drawing on it, a list of seven with five bars apiece, and the carousel it is now. What the list bought was reading two hulls against each other; what it cost was seeing either of them, and what a hull looks like is most of what a pilot is choosing between. See decision 113. Nothing in body costs a credit on the shipped roster: every hull's flight step is zero.

Flair is the pair the settings page is holding for the ship, the wake and which key throws which charge. They went there because a panel a player opens to spend credits was the wrong home for two things that cost nothing. A section that costs nothing sits fine beside four that do, so they come back here and settings loses them: one control, one home.

The choice that was open, and two small ones.

Chris took the contents. AltReading is the record of the other one: a section reading the credits standing in it, which is the same currency the tray is denominated in, so the two read as one instrument and a pilot hunting a credit to free knows which row to open without opening any. What it cannot do is say anything about the ship, and the pilot is here about a gun.

Small: reset stays on the menu, because what it puts back is all five sections at once. A reset inside each section is the other reading and is not drawn here.

Small: the level row is called Level. It was Rung, which is the client's word rather than the core's; SIM_SLOT_LEVEL and SLOT_NOTES both say level.
